title: Biofuel Production Overview
desc: Understand how biofuels are made from crops, waste and algae, with sustainability, safety, cost and policy.
outcomes: Explain biofuel types and basic production steps.
Do simple mass and energy balances.
Write a balanced overview for a community or investor.
task: Produce a three-page overview of one biofuel pathway with process chart, balance, emissions estimate, risks and recommendation.
condition: A computer, public data, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. No production work is done.
standard: Process steps and balances are correct; emissions use stated assumptions; risks and safety are listed; sources dated; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Students, farm cooperatives, energy staff, policy assistants.
evidence: process chart, balance sheet, emissions estimate, overview
modules: Types of biofuel
Understand
Biofuels are fuels made from biological materials.
Ethanol is made by fermenting sugars or starch and is blended with petrol.
Biodiesel is made from oils and fats and is blended with diesel.
Biogas is made by digesting wet waste and is used for cooking, heat or power.
Advanced biofuels use residues, wood or algae and are mostly at pilot scale.
Waste cooking oil can be converted to biodiesel using alcohol and a catalyst, and then tested for water and acidity before use.
Make a table of five biofuels with feedstock, product and use.
Each type is accurate and sourced.
Feedstocks
Analyse
What you start with matters for cost and sustainability.
Food crops, crop residues, used oils, energy crops and wet waste.
Compare yield per hectare, cost and competition with food.
Prefer wastes and residues over new land use.
Check supply is reliable.
Used cooking oil collected from restaurants avoids new land use; sugarcane gives high ethanol yield but needs water and land.
Compare four feedstocks.
Pros and cons for each with a source.
Production steps
Understand
Each pathway has a chain of steps.
Collect and clean the feedstock; convert; separate; purify; store.
Fermentation makes ethanol, a chemical reaction makes biodiesel, digestion makes biogas.
Co-products such as glycerol and digestate can be sold or reused.
Quality tests guard against engine damage.
In a biogas digester, food waste breaks down in the absence of air, producing methane-rich gas and nutrient-rich digestate used as fertiliser.
Draw a process chart for one pathway with inputs, outputs and co-products.
Chart shows all steps and outputs.
Mass and energy balance
Apply
Check the numbers for a simple process.
Inputs equal outputs plus losses.
Energy ratio = energy out / energy in.
Water use per litre produced.
Use consistent units.
100 kg of oil plus 20 kg of alcohol gives about 95 kg of biodiesel and 10 kg of glycerol, with 15 kg of losses and residue.
Calculate a simple balance for your pathway.
Totals reconcile and units are consistent.
Emissions and sustainability
Evaluate
A biofuel is cleaner only if the whole chain is clean.
Count land change, fertiliser, processing energy, transport and use.
Compare with fossil fuel per megajoule.
Use a recognised method and state boundaries.
Consider water and biodiversity.
Waste-based biodiesel can cut life-cycle emissions greatly. A fuel from newly cleared forest land may increase them.
Do a simple emissions estimate and list assumptions.
Method and sources listed.
Safety and quality
Apply
Fuels burn and chemicals harm.
Flammable liquids, methanol, strong bases and acids need controls.
Quality tests: water content, acidity, flash point and viscosity.
Storage, earthing and spill plans.
Training and personal protective equipment.
A spill kit, earthing straps and a no-ignition zone are set up around the storage tank.
List hazards and controls for your pathway.
Each hazard has a control.
Economics and policy
Evaluate
Costs, incentives and fairness decide success.
Feedstock is often the largest cost.
Blend mandates and incentives change prices.
Fair prices for farmers and no food shortages.
Local jobs and energy security.
A blending rule increases demand for used oil, so collection networks grow and a small processor becomes profitable.
Cost one pathway with a price per litre.
Currency shown and assumptions listed.
Write the overview
Create
Combine your findings into a balanced recommendation.
Summary, evidence, risks and next steps.
State what you do not know.
Test with a reader.
Update as data changes.
The note recommends starting with biogas from market waste, a pathway with low land use and local benefit.
Finish and present.
Reader can repeat the recommendation and a main risk.
